title: Panel: Goldman Sachs' laughable rebrand, does new study reveal UBI's benefits?
description: Team Rising investigates a new study on UBI and the efforts by Goldman Sachs' to rebrand their wealth.  About Rising:  Rising is a weekday morning show with bipartisan hosts that breaks the mold of morning TV by taking viewers inside the halls of Washington power like never before. The show leans into the day's political cycle with cutting edge analysis from DC insiders who can predict what is going to happen. It also sets the day's political agenda by breaking exclusive news with a team of scoop-driven reporters and demanding answers during interviews with the country's most important political newsmakers.   Follow Rising on social media:  Website: Hill.TV  Facebook: facebook.com/HillTVLive/  Instagram: @HillTVLive  Twitter: @HillTVLive  Follow Saagar Enjeti & Krystal Ball on social media:  Twitter: @esaagar and @krystalball  Instagram: @esaagar and @krystalmball

asr.full_text: GEOFF BENNETT, JR.: Goldman Sachs is rearing its head in this Democratic primary, and a new study may reveal the benefits of universal basic income. HANNAH HART, TEAM RISING, is here to weigh in on all of this. Michael Starr Hopkins is a Democratic strategist, and Marshall Kosloff is a media analyst. Gentlemen, great to have you. Thanks. Good to see you guys. All right, so interesting new article here from the Washington Post. Basically, Goldman Sachs, they've launched this thing, a small business initiative. But the more important thing is they're holding candidate forums all across some of these early states, and it's headed by a lobbyist for the financial industry. And what those lobbyists are doing are basically luring candidates like Kamala Harris into these presidential forums. So, I mean, Michael, it's just funny because, hey, good rebrand for them, right? 10,000 small businesses, even though you're a massive multinational financial conglomerate. But, I mean, it's not very wise for candidates to be going to these things in the year 2019. I was just gonna say I don't know what candidates are really going to these things and really want to have that photo op. The ones who just need somewhere to be. Have a hole in their schedule. You know Goldman is notorious for kind of you know being the villain of the financial industry so you know any candidate that really shows up there is kind of clutching at straws and doesn't really know where the base of the financial industry. So any candidate that really shows up there is kind of clutching at straws and doesn't really know where the base of the party is at. I do think it shares a more interesting thing. I've talked about this on the show earlier. You see Goldman, you see Business Roundtable and all these other massive lobbying organizations for financial companies. They're like, listen, we get it. Class war, it's out of control. Here is our ethical corporatism that they're trying to put forward. What do you think of that, Marshall, and how it all comes together in the primary? So what we should probably do here is slap a new coat of paint on it, give it a new name, and then basically people will be down for the current system. Once again, it just shows this case of, in of, I don't think people are actually getting it. I think that people are looking, and this is the problem with all these narratives, right? People are sort of thinking, capitalism has a branding problem. So what we need to use is new names, like common capitalism, you know, pro-fun capitalism, small business week, hashtag. It's capitalism for those who want it. Yeah, it's missing the point. That's why we're dunking on it. And when Goldman talks about small businesses, they're not talking about the mom and pop bookstore that has been open for 50 years. They're talking about a company worth like $50 million. Even if they are talking about that mom and pop bookstore, it's all just window dressing. It's all just to whitewash their image and try to improve their brand. I mean, I do think there is somewhat of a recognition among the ruling class that things have gone a little too far. So they want to at least have some appearance of, some window dressing, some, oh, maybe we'd support like, a half a penny wealth tax. There is a little bit of that thinking. So I don't think people are expecting sort of the elite of the Democratic Party to sit down and shut up forever.
